title: Data and data analysis: foundations, security and dilemmas
scope: 3.1A–I · supplied chapter pp. 57–80 · four teaching arcs; choose to fit prior learning

slides.title: Data records part of a situation
lines: A click records an action
A system may infer a preference from that action
The inference remains open to other explanations
slides.notes: A viewer might watch a video because they enjoy it, need it for a class or disagree with it. The recorded action is not identical to the viewer’s reason. Data analytics uses observations to find patterns or make predictions. We begin by distinguishing a recorded value from an inference. This matters when a platform decides what to show next. Our examples use invented records. We will not collect personal histories or require students to enter accounts to explore the mechanism.
slides.prompt: Identify three kinds of data in the scene. Which reason for watching would remain an inference?
slides.source_note: Bomfim et al., Digital Society for the IB Diploma, Hodder, 2022. Printed pages cited per slide. Original paraphrase. Textbook connection: pp. 72–73.
slides.alt: Conceptual AI sports scene: sensor, camera, ticket scan and phone contribute different data to storage. No real venue or measured outcomes.

slides.title: One reading becomes four different claims
lines: Context and judgement add meaning; more data alone is not wisdom.
slides.prompt: In 2 minutes, distinguish data from information using a new rainfall example. Then explain what extra reasoning a decision requires.
slides.notes: Purpose: Context and judgement add meaning; more data alone is not wisdom. Say: A number without a unit, place or time is hard to interpret. Information adds those relationships. Knowledge draws a usable conclusion; wisdom weighs a course of action and its limits. A sensor cannot settle the safety decision by itself. Ask: In 2 minutes, distinguish data from information using a new rainfall example. Then explain what extra reasoning a decision requires. Practice feedback: use the worked exhibit to check the distinction; keep the first attempt and append a correction. Secure: apply the distinction to a different venue. Partial: isolate the disputed operation and compare the two cases. Unclear: reconstruct the first worked example before retrying. Later return: next lesson, close notes and explain this distinction in a library or community-centre system. These are formative practice responses, not registered assessment items.

slides.title: The question determines which data you need
lines: Quantitative and qualitative data describe different aspects of a situation.
slides.prompt: Name a qualitative and a quantitative record for a fictional shop. Explain why neither alone establishes customer satisfaction.
slides.notes: Purpose: Quantitative and qualitative data describe different aspects of a situation. Say: Financial, medical, meteorological, geographical and scientific are context categories. Quantitative values support numerical comparisons; qualitative descriptions convey experiences and meanings. Scientific data can be unpublished observations as well as published research; publication is not what makes a measurement data. Ask: Name a qualitative and a quantitative record for a fictional shop. Explain why neither alone establishes customer satisfaction. Practice feedback: use the worked exhibit to check the distinction; keep the first attempt and append a correction. Secure: apply the distinction to a different venue. slides.title: A photo has content and metadata
lines: Metadata can reveal something the visible image does not.
slides.prompt: A student removes their face from an image but leaves location metadata. Explain one remaining privacy risk.
slides.notes: Purpose: Metadata can reveal something the visible image does not. Say: The pixels are the visible content. Descriptive fields help systems organize and interpret a file. Removing a visible person does not necessarily remove location or date records. Metadata can be useful and sensitive at the same time. Ask: A student removes their face from an image but leaves location metadata. Explain one remaining privacy risk. slides.title: Find a pattern, or link records about an entity?
lines: Data mining and data matching answer different questions.
slides.prompt: A shop joins returns to purchases and then looks for repeated return patterns. Name each operation and one limitation.
slides.notes: Purpose: Data mining and data matching answer different questions. Say: Matching identifies which records refer to the same entity. Mining investigates patterns or anomalies within records. The operations can be combined, but a mistaken match can contaminate the pattern. Association does not establish cause. Ask: A shop joins returns to purchases and then looks for repeated return patterns. Name each operation and one limitation. Practice feedback: use the worked exhibit to check the distinction; keep the first attempt and append a correction. Secure: apply the distinction to a different venue. slides.title: Five stages manage a record over time
lines: Preservation and destruction are distinct decisions.
slides.prompt: Identify two decisions at different stages that could protect a participant. Explain why simply keeping everything is not a plan.
slides.notes: Purpose: Preservation and destruction are distinct decisions. Say: Creation can be manual or automatic. Storage concerns location, permissions and protection. Usage transforms or shares data. Preservation maintains suitable data for a stated future need. Destruction requires a method that fits the media and all relevant copies. Ask: Identify two decisions at different stages that could protect a participant. Explain why simply keeping everything is not a plan. Practice feedback: use the worked exhibit to check the distinction; keep the first attempt and append a correction. Secure: apply the distinction to a different venue. Partial: isolate the disputed operation and compare the two cases. Unclear: reconstruct the first worked example before retrying. Later return: next lesson, close notes and explain this distinction in a library or community-centre system. These are formative practice responses, not registered assessment items.

slides.title: Primary or secondary depends on the investigation
lines: The relationship to collection matters, not whether the file is online.
slides.prompt: A school downloads a dataset originally collected by a weather agency. Explain its status for each organization and one reuse limitation.
slides.notes: Purpose: The relationship to collection matters, not whether the file is online. Say: Original collection for the current purpose is primary. Reuse of data someone else collected is secondary. Check methods, date, units and population before using it for a changed purpose; online versus paper does not settle the distinction. Ask: A school downloads a dataset originally collected by a weather agency. Explain its status for each organization and one reuse limitation. Practice feedback: use the worked exhibit to check the distinction; keep the first attempt and append a correction. Secure: apply the distinction to a different venue. slides.title: An entity becomes records with typed fields
lines: A database schema states what each field can hold.
slides.prompt: Choose suitable fields/types for a fictional event booking. Explain why a telephone number should not be treated as a quantity.
slides.notes: Purpose: A database schema states what each field can hold. Say: Entities are things represented by the system. Attributes are properties of them. Fields store those attributes, with types such as integer, floating point, string, character, Boolean or date. Digits can be identifiers: leading zeros and formatting matter for a phone number. Ask: Choose suitable fields/types for a fictional event booking. Explain why a telephone number should not be treated as a quantity. slides.title: Keys link entities without repeating every detail
lines: The primary key identifies a record; a foreign key refers to another table.
slides.prompt: Explain the BookID link in your own words. What fails if two books share the same primary key?
slides.notes: Purpose: The primary key identifies a record; a foreign key refers to another table. Say: A unique key avoids ambiguity. A foreign key records a relationship. One book can have many loan records; the book title need not be copied into every loan. Wrong or missing links undermine integrity even if every value has a valid type. Ask: Explain the BookID link in your own words. What fails if two books share the same primary key? slides.title: Suitable is different from accurately copied
lines: A valid value can still be the wrong value.
slides.prompt: A date passes the allowed format but was copied from the wrong row. Which check passed, which is needed, and why?
slides.notes: Purpose: A valid value can still be the wrong value. Say: Validation checks permitted form or range: type, length, input mask, range or lookup. Verification compares entry with the intended source or a second entry. Neither guarantees the source itself is true. Explain the exact error each can detect. Ask: A date passes the allowed format but was copied from the wrong row. Which check passed, which is needed, and why? slides.prompt: Which event record should volunteers see: attendance count or a health request? Explain a purpose-based access decision.

lines: A chart needs a suitable comparison, units and honest scale.

slides.notes: Purpose: A chart needs a suitable comparison, units and honest scale. Say: Tables preserve exact values; charts emphasize a relationship. slides.title: Encryption changes readable data into ciphertext
lines: Symmetric encryption uses the same secret key to encrypt and decrypt.
slides.prompt: If an attacker obtains both ciphertext and the secret key, explain why the protection is weakened.
slides.notes: Purpose: Symmetric encryption uses the same secret key to encrypt and decrypt. Say: Encryption protects confidentiality by transforming data under a key. The authorized party recovers plaintext. It does not make the original record accurate or decide who should be permitted to use it. A Caesar cipher can demonstrate substitution but is not modern security. Ask: If an attacker obtains both ciphertext and the secret key, explain why the protection is weakened. Practice feedback: use the worked exhibit to check the distinction; keep the first attempt and append a correction. Secure: apply the distinction to a different venue. Partial: isolate the disputed operation and compare the two cases. Unclear: reconstruct the first worked example before retrying. Later return: next lesson, close notes and explain this distinction in a library or community-centre system. These are formative practice responses, not registered assessment items.

slides.title: Public-key encryption separates the two key roles
lines: Encrypt for the recipient with their public key; decrypt with their private key.
slides.prompt: Whose public key should a sender use for a confidential message to a recipient? Explain who holds the private key and why it stays secret.
slides.notes: Purpose: Encrypt for the recipient with their public key; decrypt with their private key. Say: The recipient shares their public key while retaining the private key. Do not teach that the sender shares the recipient’s private key. Modern secure connections combine asymmetric key establishment/authentication and symmetric protection; SSL is historical terminology, TLS is the current protocol family. Ask: Whose public key should a sender use for a confidential message to a recipient? Explain who holds the private key and why it stays secret. Practice feedback: use the worked exhibit to check the distinction; keep the first attempt and append a correction. Secure: apply the distinction to a different venue. Partial: isolate the disputed operation and compare the two cases. Unclear: reconstruct the first worked example before retrying. Later return: next lesson, close notes and explain this distinction in a library or community-centre system. These are formative practice responses, not registered assessment items.

slides.title: Masking and encryption solve different problems
lines: Replacing visible details does not automatically remove re-identification risk.
slides.prompt: A dataset removes names but keeps exact home locations and rare diagnoses. Explain why “anonymous” needs further evidence.
slides.notes: Purpose: Replacing visible details does not automatically remove re-identification risk. Say: Masking substitutes or obscures selected values for a purpose such as software testing. Encryption is reversible with the relevant key. Neither by itself proves anonymity. Evaluate what remains and what can be linked; do not promise that name removal guarantees privacy. Ask: A dataset removes names but keeps exact home locations and rare diagnoses. Explain why “anonymous” needs further evidence. slides.title: Deletion is not a disposal guarantee
lines: Choose sanitization for the storage medium, sensitivity and required assurance.
slides.prompt: A school is retiring an SSD containing confidential records. Explain why “delete the folder” is insufficient and what an authorized technician must verify.
slides.notes: Purpose: Choose sanitization for the storage medium, sensitivity and required assurance. Say: Destruction is a lifecycle decision; sanitization is the method and verification. A recycle bin, a pointer deletion or an ordinary format does not necessarily sanitize all storage. Degaussing concerns suitable magnetic media, not an SSD. Students analyse the decision; they must not erase school devices. Ask: A school is retiring an SSD containing confidential records. slides.title: A linked ledger protects record history, not truth at entry
lines: Hash links and network agreement make some changes detectable or difficult.
slides.prompt: A seafood supplier enters a false catch location into a ledger. Explain what a blockchain could protect and what it cannot establish.
slides.notes: Purpose: Hash links and network agreement make some changes detectable or difficult. Say: A distributed ledger is replicated across participants. Cryptographic links and consensus rules resist undetected alteration of accepted history. They do not certify a real-world claim before entry. slides.title: Big data and data analytics
lines: Big data involves large, varied collections of records
Analytics processes data to find patterns and trends
A useful result depends on the question and the quality of the data
slides.notes: The textbook characterizes big data using four Vs. Data can be structured in a table or arrive in formats such as video, text and images. Analytics can describe what happened, detect patterns or support a prediction. A classroom table is small data, but it helps us reason about a process that operates on a much larger collection. A numerical output is not automatically a reliable answer. Ask how the records were collected, what they represent and how the analysis matches the question.
slides.prompt: Which of the four Vs can a very large dataset still fail?

slides.title: Volume and velocity
lines: Volume describes the amount of data
Velocity describes how quickly data arrives and is processed
Fast incoming data can create processing and checking demands
slides.notes: Consider a match where sensors generate records throughout play. Volume concerns how many records accumulate. Velocity concerns the rate at which new records arrive and whether analysis can keep up. A system that stores a large archive may have high volume without fast current arrival. A live stream may require quick decisions before every record can be manually checked. Explain which characteristic matters to a particular task instead of treating big data as a single vague advantage.

lines: Variety concerns formats and types of data
Veracity concerns accuracy, reliability and quality
A larger collection can contain more of the same error
slides.notes: A platform may combine a video, its caption, a device setting and an interaction log. These are different kinds of data. That variety creates opportunities, but joining formats accurately can be difficult. Veracity concerns whether the values are trustworthy for the intended use. Repeated records, missing values, outdated labels and false accounts can all distort an analysis. Having many formats does not establish good quality. A large dataset can remain unrepresentative even when its individual records are accurate.

quiz.q: A million records contain the same incorrect duration unit. Which V is directly affected?
quiz.why: An incorrect unit undermines the accuracy and usefulness of the recorded values.

slides.title: Small and clean, or large and messy?
lines: Dataset A: 40 verified records from one class
Dataset B: 40,000 records with duplicates and missing fields
Neither size alone nor cleanliness alone answers the question
slides.notes: These invented datasets force us to name a purpose. Dataset A may be suitable for checking one class’s activity, but it may not represent the whole school. Dataset B might capture a wider range of people, yet its errors require investigation. We cannot decide which is better without knowing the question, sampling, missingness and quality controls. Data cleaning can improve validity while accidentally removing groups if missing values are unevenly distributed. Make the decision and its assumption visible.
slides.prompt: Which would you use to describe your class? What would you need to describe the whole school?
slides.source_note: Bomfim et al., Digital Society for the IB Diploma, Hodder, 2022. Printed pages cited per slide. Original paraphrase. Textbook connection: pp. 73–74.

slides.title: A missing value is an unresolved question
lines: Blank duration does not mean zero duration
Dropping a record changes who remains in the dataset
Imputing a value introduces an assumption
slides.notes: Suppose an item has no completion value. Replacing it with zero can push the creator down the ranking even though zero completion was never observed. Removing the item avoids the calculation but also removes its opportunity for exposure. Estimating a value may help, yet it relies on an assumption that needs checking. A sensible choice depends on the task and consequence. Record what you chose and how the result might change under another plausible choice.
slides.prompt: Compare exclusion with estimation for a new creator. State one uncertainty for each.
slides.source_note: Bomfim et al., Digital Society for the IB Diploma, Hodder, 2022. Printed pages cited per slide. Original paraphrase. Textbook connection: pp. 73–74.

slides.title: An association does not establish a cause
lines: A pattern may be useful for prediction
Other factors may explain the relationship
A causal conclusion needs an appropriate investigation
slides.notes: Items with more exposure often receive more interactions. This could reflect relevance, the number of opportunities to be seen or both. Looking only at interaction totals cannot distinguish those explanations. A carefully designed comparison might hold exposure constant or compare a changed allocation, but even then we need to examine other factors and limits. The important habit is to state the measured relationship first, then ask which alternative explanations the evidence has ruled out.
slides.prompt: Why might comparing reactions per exposure help? What uncertainty would remain?
slides.source_note: Bomfim et al., Digital Society for the IB Diploma, Hodder, 2022. Printed pages cited per slide. Original paraphrase. Textbook connection: pp. 73.
slides.alt: Teaching diagram: An association does not establish a cause. Its relationships are explained in the visible transcript.

slides.title: The data lifecycle creates decisions at every stage
lines: Create or collect data
Store and use it
Preserve or destroy it when appropriate
slides.notes: The chapter places big data inside a lifecycle. At collection, we decide what to record and whom to include. Storage involves access, security and organization. Use involves analysis and sharing for a purpose. Preservation and destruction concern how long records remain and what happens when they are no longer needed. This week’s assigned reading begins the collection dilemmas in section 3.1I. It does not teach all later lifecycle dilemmas. A diagram of a lifecycle is a map, not proof that every stage has been adequately managed.

quiz.q: Why does a lifecycle model matter?
options: Decisions about collection, use and retention can each affect people
Data should always be retained forever
quiz.why: Different stages introduce different decisions and responsibilities.

slides.source_note: Bomfim et al., Digital Society for the IB Diploma, Hodder, 2022. Printed pages cited per slide. Original paraphrase. Textbook connection: pp. 72, 74.

slides.title: Collection can shape the eventual result
lines: Collect data that fits a defined purpose
Examine whose records are absent or overrepresented
Consider permission and unnecessary collection
slides.notes: The assigned page raises ethical collection, consent and excessive collection. We can ask what information is actually needed to answer a question, and whether a group is missing before analysis begins. Collecting an additional personal detail can create a privacy cost without improving the decision. Applicable rules depend on the setting and jurisdiction, so this is an ethical design discussion rather than a universal legal checklist. Explain the purpose, the proposed data and the effect of collecting or omitting it.
slides.prompt: Does a school discovery feed need a student’s legal name to test a ranking? Explain your decision.
slides.source_note: Bomfim et al., Digital Society for the IB Diploma, Hodder, 2022. Printed pages cited per slide. Original paraphrase. Textbook connection: pp. 74.

slides.title: Analytics can support several purposes
lines: Describe a past pattern
Detect an unusual record or event
Predict a possible future outcome
slides.notes: The textbook gives historical examples from finance and sports. The enduring idea is the use of data to inform a decision. Describing last month’s activity, flagging an unusual transaction and predicting interest are different tasks. A prediction expresses an estimated outcome and should be evaluated against later observations. The examples do not make analytics infallible. A false alert can inconvenience someone, while a missed alert can leave a problem undetected. Identify the task and the cost of each kind of error.
slides.prompt: Choose one purpose and identify a false positive and a false negative in a school context.
slides.source_note: Bomfim et al., Digital Society for the IB Diploma, Hodder, 2022. Printed pages cited per slide. Original paraphrase. Textbook connection: pp. 73.

slides.title: A bounded big-data inquiry
lines: Question: whose experience does this dataset describe?
Check collection, formats, missing records and quality
Match each claim to evidence that can support it
slides.notes: A manageable inquiry identifies a particular use rather than asking whether all big data is good. For a platform, we could investigate whether recorded interactions represent new creators as well as established ones. The real case file gives a provider account and a regulator account with different purposes. Neither offers a complete dataset of individual experiences. Use the source passport to record the locator, claim, evidence and limitation. A limitation helps you decide what a source is useful for rather than simply dismissing it as biased.
slides.prompt: Draft a focused question and identify one missing piece of evidence.
slides.source_note: Bomfim et al., Digital Society for the IB Diploma, Hodder, 2022. Printed pages cited per slide. Original paraphrase. Textbook connection: pp. 74.

slides.title: Reliability and integrity are separate tests
lines: Accurate, complete data can become unreliable through unauthorized changes.
slides.prompt: A telephone number is outdated; a second record was maliciously changed. Explain each problem and a different corrective action.
slides.notes: Purpose: Accurate, complete data can become unreliable through unauthorized changes. Say: Update, verify and evaluate sources to improve reliability. Control access and track alterations to protect integrity. Biased sampling, stale records, malware and entry errors can cause different failures. Automatic collection removes some manual errors but introduces others. Ask: A telephone number is outdated; a second record was maliciously changed. Explain each problem and a different corrective action. Practice feedback: use the worked exhibit to check the distinction; keep the first attempt and append a correction. Secure: apply the distinction to a different venue. Partial: isolate the disputed operation and compare the two cases. Unclear: reconstruct the first worked example before retrying. Later return: next lesson, close notes and explain this distinction in a library or community-centre system. These are formative practice responses, not registered assessment items.

slides.title: Privacy and anonymity are different conditions
lines: A person can be identifiable while their information remains restricted.
slides.prompt: Explain how a named record can be private and an unnamed post can reveal a person. Name one protection beyond removing a name.
slides.notes: Purpose: A person can be identifiable while their information remains restricted. Say: Anonymity concerns whether someone can be identified; privacy concerns access, use, surveillance and control. Legitimate advice or expression may need protection. Accountability and safety may create competing demands; judge a specific use, not all anonymity. Ask: Explain how a named record can be private and an unnamed post can reveal a person. lines: Purpose, minimization and accuracy constrain the data pipeline.
slides.prompt: An event form requests birth date and later sells an advertising list. Identify two relevant principles and justify an improvement.

slides.title: Retention and responsibility finish the protection plan
lines: A protection promise needs a retention rule, safeguards and accountable decisions.
slides.prompt: Explain why “keep it forever in case it is useful” needs challenge. Name one record the organization should keep about its own decisions.
slides.notes: Purpose: A protection promise needs a retention rule, safeguards and accountable decisions.
